Observational unit, variable, value, population, sample: definitions (statistical study terminology)
column2:
Observational unit: entity measured
Variable: feature that can differ across units
Value: one recorded outcome for one unit
Population: group the research question refers to
Sample: units actually observed

column1: Suitable summary metrics per variable type (nominal, ordinal, discrete numeric, continuous numeric)
column2:
Nominal categorical: counts, proportions
Ordinal categorical: ordered counts, median (order, no guaranteed equal spacing)
Discrete numeric: mean or distribution
Continuous numeric: mean, spread, shape

column1: Mode, median, mean: definitions and properties (measures of central tendency)
column2:
Mode: most frequent score; can be bimodal/multimodal
Median: middle score of ordered data; robust to extremes
Mean: average of all scores; uses all data; sensitive to outliers

column1: Variance, standard deviation (SD), range, interquartile range (IQR): definitions, formulas, robustness; boxplot outlier fences
column2:
Variance: average squared deviation from mean, $s^2=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$
SD: $\sqrt{s^2}$
Range: max − min; affected by extremes
IQR: $Q3-Q1$; robust to outliers
Fences: $Q1-1.5\cdot IQR$, $Q3+1.5\cdot IQR$; points beyond = outliers

column1: Distribution shape: skew types, kurtosis (formula, reference value, terms), formal normality tests
column2:
Positive skew: tail on right; negative skew: tail on left
Kurtosis $=\frac{\frac1n\sum(x_i-\bar x)^4}{\left[\frac1n\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\right]^2}$
Normal ≈ 3; >3 leptokurtic (heavy tails, pointy); <3 platykurtic (light tails, flat)
Tests: Shapiro-Wilk, Kolmogorov-Smirnov

column1: Basic probability rules: bounds of $P(A)$, $P(\Omega)$, complement $P(A^c)$, union $P(A\cup B)$
column2:
$0\le P(A)\le1$
$P(\Omega)=1$ (sample space)
$P(A^c)=1-P(A)$
Addition rule: $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$

column1: Conditional probability, product rule, Bayes' rule: formulas; components of Bayes' rule
column2:
$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$, $P(B)>0$; restricts reference group to cases with B; generally $P(A\mid B)\neq P(B\mid A)$
Product: $P(A,B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)=P(A\mid B)P(B)$
Bayes: $P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}$
Components: prior $P(A)$; likelihood $P(B\mid A)$; normalisation $P(B)$ over all explanations of B

column1: Independence vs. mutual exclusivity of events X and Y: definitions, formulas, relation
column2:
Independence: knowing X does not change P(Y); $P(Y\mid X)=P(Y)$ ⇔ $P(X\cap Y)=P(X)P(Y)$
Mutually exclusive: cannot occur together; $X\cap Y=\emptyset$, $P(X\cap Y)=0$, so $P(X\cup Y)=P(X)+P(Y)$
Not the same concept

column1: Probability mass function (PMF) vs. probability density function (PDF): use, definition, properties
column2:
PMF: discrete variables; $p(x)=P(X=x)$; $\sum p(x)=1$
PDF: continuous variables; $P(X=x)=0$ for exact values; probability = area: $P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b p(x)\,dx$; $\int p(x)\,dx=1$; height can exceed 1

column1: Bernoulli, Binomial, Poisson: typical use, PMF, mean, variance (discrete distributions)
column2:
Bernoulli(p): single binary trial; $p^x(1-p)^{1-x}$, $x\in\{0,1\}$; mean $p$; var $p(1-p)$
Binomial(n,p): successes in n independent trials; $\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$; mean $np$; var $np(1-p)$
Poisson(λ): count in fixed interval at constant rate; $\frac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}$; mean = var = $\lambda$

column1: Exponential, Normal, Uniform $U(a,b)$: typical use, PDF, mean, variance (continuous distributions)
column2:
Exponential(λ): time between events; $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, $x\ge0$; mean $1/\lambda$; var $1/\lambda^2$
Normal $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$: symmetric bell; $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$; mean $\mu$; var $\sigma^2$
Uniform: equal probability over $[a,b]$; $\frac{1}{b-a}$; mean $\frac{a+b}{2}$; var $\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}$

column1: Sampling distribution and standard error (SE): definitions, formulas; difference SD vs. SE
column2:
Sampling distribution: distribution of sample means from same population; mean of sample means = $\mu$
SE: SD of sample means; $\sigma_{\bar x}=\sigma/\sqrt n$, estimated $s/\sqrt n$; larger n → smaller SE → more precise estimate
SD: spread among observations, $s=\sqrt{\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2/(n-1)}$
SE: sampling variability of $\bar x$

column1: Central Limit Theorem (CLT): conditions, statement, misconception, importance
column2:
Conditions: i.i.d. observations, finite $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$
$\frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\to N(0,1)$; large n: $\bar X\approx N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$
Raw data do NOT become normal; also works for discrete variables (e.g. Bernoulli averages); n often need not be very large
Importance: generalise sample → population; justifies CIs and hypothesis tests

column1: t-distribution vs. normal distribution; z-test vs. t-test: properties and when to use which
column2:
t: bell-shaped, symmetric, heavier tails; σ not assumed known; useful for small samples; → normal as df (n) increase
Rule of thumb: N > 30 normal approximation; N < 30 t
z-test: σ known or large n; $z=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$
t-test: σ unknown (use s), smaller n; $t=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}$

column1: Confidence interval (CI): definition, general form, mean with unknown σ, 95% steps, interpretation, width meaning
column2:
Boundaries within which true mean believed to lie
Estimate ± critical value × SE; unknown σ: $\bar x\pm t_{(n-1,\,0.975)}\cdot s/\sqrt n$
95%: $\alpha=0.05$, $\alpha/2=0.025$, $z_{\alpha/2}=1.96$, $\bar x\pm1.96\cdot SE$
Repeated 100×: ~95 CIs contain $\mu$, ~5 do not
Narrow = high precision; wide = more uncertainty; links to hypothesis testing

column1: Hypothesis testing: key question, general procedure, test statistic (definition, concept, examples)
column2:
Key question: observed pattern due to chance or real effect?
Steps: 1 state $H_0$ vs $H_a$; 2 check assumptions (random sample, independence, normality or large n); 3 compute test statistic; 4 find p-value (tail area); 5 compare p with α
Test statistic: distance of result from $H_0$ in SE units, (estimate − null value)/SE
Concept: systematic (model-explained) / unsystematic (error) variation; >1 = explained exceeds error
Examples: t, F, $\chi^2$; known distributions under $H_0$

column1: p-value: definition, right-tailed and two-tailed formulas, interpretation
column2:
Probability of result as or more extreme than observed, assuming $H_0$ true
Right-tailed: $P(T\ge t_{obs}\mid H_0)$
Two-tailed: $P(|T|\ge|t_{obs}|\mid H_0)$
Small p = evidence against $H_0$; further into tail = stronger evidence
Not $P(H_0$ true$)$; not effect size/importance

column1: Test statistic formulas: one-sample mean, two-sample means, one-proportion, two-proportion tests (incl. df, variance options, validity conditions)
column2:
One-sample: $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$; $t=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}$, df $=n-1$; z if σ known
Two-sample: $H_0:\mu_1-\mu_2=0$; $t=\frac{\bar x_1-\bar x_2}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}$; Welch df default; pooled variance if equal variances (standard test assumes equal variances)
One-proportion: $z=\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}$; valid if $np_0\ge10$, $n(1-p_0)\ge10$
Two-proportion: pooled $\hat p=\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}$; $z=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}$

column1: Type I error, Type II error, statistical power: definitions, typical values, decision table, factors increasing power, error trade-off
column2:
Type I (α): false positive; typically 0.05; $H_0$ true but rejected
Type II (β): false negative, missing real effect; typically 0.20 (~1 in 5 missed); $H_0$ false but not rejected
Correct: $H_0$ true not rejected; $H_0$ false rejected = power $1-\beta$
Power ↑: larger true effect; larger n; less unexplained variability / efficient design; less strict α
Defined for specific test, effect, n, data-generating model
Lower α → fewer false positives but less power; larger n → more power without raising α

column1: Effect size: definition, four common measures, relation to statistical significance
column2:
Magnitude of difference/association, not just whether significant
Mean difference (original units); Cohen's d (difference in SD units); Pearson's r (direction, strength of linear association); odds ratio (relative odds, binary outcome)
Significance ≠ scientific importance; report estimate with CI, interpret in context
Study planning: meaningful effect size, acceptable α, n for adequate power
